title: Weddings
hook: vows before God and witnesses: for better, for worse

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing, and the word benediction: hands raised over a room, and the people sent out the door. Your line was go in peace. Who did you send off with a good word? Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

"Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." That's how the old English prayer book opens a wedding. In front, two people who didn't sleep much last night. Beside them, a best man patting his pocket for the third time to check the rings are still there. In the second row, a grandmother who has been crying since the processional. Behind her, a cousin filming everything. In a few minutes, two people will say out loud, in front of all of them, that they'll stay through the good years and the terrible ones. Today: weddings.

A Christian wedding is a promise made in two directions at once: to each other, and before God. Start with the witnesses. The prayer book says "in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." The people in the pews aren't an audience. They're there to see the promise made, and to remember it. Then the vows themselves. In the prayer book, each one promises "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." Those words aren't in the Bible. They come from the prayer book. And look at what they do: they name the worse before it arrives. Nobody at the altar knows what's coming. The vow says yes to it anyway. Then the scripture that's often read. Genesis says a man will "leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh," and in Matthew, Jesus quotes it. In John's Gospel, Jesus is at a wedding in Cana when the wine runs out, and John calls what he does there the beginning of his miracles. And some couples choose Ruth's promise, "whither thou goest, I will go," which in the story Ruth says to Naomi, her mother-in-law. Churches understand the wedding differently. Catholics call marriage a sacrament, and in Catholic teaching the bride and groom are themselves its ministers: they marry each other, and the priest witnesses. The Orthodox call it a holy mystery, and crowns are placed on, or held over, the couple's heads. Protestant churches that keep two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, honor marriage as holy without counting it as a third.
screen: `THE VOW NAMES THE WORSE IN ADVANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a couple. Settle, and breathe. Bring one couple to mind. Newlyweds, or two people married longer than they can remember being single, or a pair going through the worse part right now. Picture them side by side. Think of one thing that's hard for them, and one thing that's good. If you pray, you can ask God to keep them in both: the better and the worse. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with goodwill, the way a witness in the pews would. The bell holds the time.
Weddings. Vows made before God and a room full of witnesses, promising in advance to stay through the better and the worse.
Your line: for better, for worse. Today, send a short note to a couple you know, and tell them one good thing you've seen in them. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Christian couples exchange vows in church before a minister or priest and the congregation as witnesses; Catholics celebrate marriage as a sacrament, the Orthodox crown the couple in the service of crowning, and Protestant churches hold a service of worship honoring marriage as holy, without counting it a sacrament.

fork.setup: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and Naomi, your mother-in-law, is going home. she tells you to go back to your own people. what do you do?
options: go back to your own family.
stay with Naomi: "whither thou goest, I will go."
fork.reveal: Ruth stays. her promise, now often heard at weddings, was first a daughter-in-law's loyalty to the woman who'd lost everything with her.

original.note: Greek: a wedding, a wedding feast, the word for the celebration at Cana in John 2:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wedding is a party for the couple.
what it means: vows made before God and witnesses, naming the worse before it comes.
what a scholar hears: "for better for worse" is prayer-book English, not scripture, and in Catholic teaching the couple themselves are the sacrament's ministers.
